title: Ayin
hookLine: ayin is an eye, and silent

cards: A young woman runs away into the desert. Her name is Hagar, a servant in Abraham's household, pregnant, and treated so harshly that she flees. The text finds her alone by a spring on the road to Shur.

There an angel of the Lord finds her too, and asks a question almost too simple: where have you come from, and where are you going? She answers honestly: she's running. Then Hagar, the outsider, does something bold.
She gives God a name. Today's letter is in it.

teach.h: AYIN: AN EYE, AND A SPRING.
teach.b: Ayin means an eye. It also means a spring, where water wells up out of the ground. So where the angel finds Hagar by a spring, the Hebrew says by the ayin of water.
Four things to see. First, the eye.

Hagar calls God El Roi, which the old Jewish Publication Society translation renders a God of seeing. Then she wonders whether she has really seen the one who sees her. The runaway in the desert is not invisible.
Someone has looked at her with care. Second, the spring. The place gets a name too: a well named for the living one who sees.
Some readers hear why an eye and a spring share a word: both are places where something rises from deep inside. Third, the silence.

teach.h: A LETTER THAT MAKES NO SOUND.
teach.b: In everyday Israeli speech, ayin usually makes no sound; the vowel carries the voice. Some Jewish communities, from Yemen and elsewhere, still sound it deep in the throat.

Either way, it can be present without making noise, a little like a good eye. Fourth, that good eye. In Pirkei Avot, Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai asks his students to go and see the good way a person should hold to.
Ayin tovah, a way of looking at people that wishes them well.
So this week ran from yud to ayin: the smallest letter, an open palm, a teacher's tall lamed, water, a fall and a lift, a hand on a shoulder, and now an eye that notices without needing to be heard.

how: Jewish children learning the alef-bet are taught that ayin means an eye; the idea of ayin tovah, a good and generous eye toward others, is taught from Pirkei Avot.

games.q: you're Hagar, alone by a spring in the desert. an angel asks where you've come from and where you're going. what does she do in the story?
o: she answers honestly, and later names God the one who sees.
she claims to be someone else.
games.why: she tells the truth, that she's fleeing, and calls God El Roi, a God of seeing.

practice: Let your eyes rest, open or closed, and bring to mind one person you see every day but rarely really look at: a neighbor, the person at the register, the one across the table.
Picture their face clearly, notice one thing you've never noticed before, and wish them one good thing without a word. If you pray, you can bring them into it.

wordCard.voice: Ayin. An eye, and a spring of water. A letter often silent, and the first letter of ayin tovah, a good eye. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: eye; also a spring of water. The name of the letter.

carryVoice: Your line: ayin is an eye. To be seen with care is a gift, even in silence. That's a week of letters.
